headline: Nvidia's CEO Returns and Says the Company Doesn't Need a Backup Leader

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Jensen Huang is the leader, or CEO, of a big computer chip company called Nvidia. He started the company a long time ago. Recently, he had to step away from his job for a little while because of some personal problems. Another leader, Colette Kress, took over for about two weeks while he was gone. Now Huang is back. At a big company meeting, he talked to everyone who works there. He said Nvidia does not need a backup plan for who would lead the company if something happened to him. He thinks having a backup plan makes companies too complicated, with too many layers of bosses. Most big companies have many different leaders in charge of different jobs. Nvidia only has five top leaders, which is much fewer than other huge companies. Huang believes this makes the company work better. But some people who own stock in the company and watch how it is run do not agree with him. They think every big company should have a plan in case the leader cannot do the job anymore. This disagreement could affect how people trust the company in the future.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Jensen Huang is the CEO, or top boss, of Nvidia, a company that makes powerful computer chips used in phones, computers, and artificial intelligence. Huang started the company himself many years ago. Recently, he stepped down from his job for a short time after admitting to some personal mistakes in his private life, including a situation involving someone the government thought might be connected to spying for China. Another executive, Colette Kress, ran the company for about 12 days while he was away. Then Huang came back to lead Nvidia again. When he returned, he held a meeting with employees to talk about what happened. He also brought up a topic that many people care about: succession planning. Succession planning means having a clear plan for who would take over if a CEO left suddenly or could not do the job anymore. Huang told employees that Nvidia does not need this kind of plan. He believes it would create unnecessary layers of bosses and management, which goes against how he built the company. Nvidia is unusual because it has very few top executives — only five — while most big companies have many more layers of leadership. Huang has said in the past that he designed the company this way on purpose, comparing it to how different kinds of businesses are organized. However, many investors and people who study businesses disagree with him. They believe that after recent events, having a backup plan would help protect the company and make people trust it more, especially since so much depends on just one person at the top.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable technology companies, known for making computer chips that power artificial intelligence. Huang recently resigned as CEO for a short period after admitting he had personal relationships outside his marriage, one of which involved a person the U.S. government suspected might be connected to espionage for China. During his short absence, Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, served as interim CEO for about 12 days. Huang has since returned to his role. When he came back, he held an all-staff meeting where he addressed the situation directly, reportedly discussing feelings of regret, his decision to seek therapy, and the company's code of conduct, which outlines expected behavior for employees and leaders. During the meeting, he also addressed a topic many people consider urgent: succession planning. This means having an official plan that explains who would take over leadership if a CEO suddenly left the company. According to a source who attended the meeting, Huang said Nvidia doesn't need this kind of plan because of the company's unusual structure. Unlike most large corporations, which have many executives and layers of management, Nvidia operates with a surprisingly small leadership team — just five executive officers in total, including Huang. He reports directly to about 60 people, cutting out many of the usual management layers. Huang argues that creating a formal succession plan would add unnecessary hierarchy, going against the very structure he intentionally built to keep the company efficient and fast-moving. He has defended this approach before, including in an interview where he criticized how many companies' leadership structures all look the same, regardless of what the company actually makes. Despite his explanation, some investors and company analysts are not convinced. They argue that after a major personal scandal that put the CEO's position at risk, having a plan in place for leadership transitions would reduce risk and reassure shareholders. This disagreement highlights a bigger question in the business world: how much power and responsibility should rest in the hands of one person, and what happens to a company if that person suddenly can't continue leading it?

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Nvidia, one of the most valuable technology companies in the world due to its dominance in AI computer chips, recently went through a leadership disruption when CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to extramarital affairs, including one involving a person the U.S. government suspected of being connected to Chinese espionage. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, stepped in as interim CEO for 12 days before Huang returned to his position. Upon his return, Huang addressed employees directly in an all-hands meeting, reportedly discussing his personal regret, his decision to attend therapy, and the company's code of conduct — the formal guidelines meant to govern employee and executive behavior. He also revisited a topic that has drawn significant attention from investors and corporate governance experts: succession planning, or the process of designating who would take over leadership if a CEO were to leave unexpectedly. According to a source who spoke with CNBC, Huang told employees that Nvidia does not need a formal succession plan because of its distinctive organizational structure. Unlike most large corporations, which typically maintain multiple layers of executives and middle management, Nvidia operates with a notably flat hierarchy. The company has only five executive officers overseeing its global operations, and Huang personally has about 60 direct reports — an unusually high number for a CEO of a company this size. Huang has defended this structure publicly before, including in a past interview where he criticized the tendency of companies across different industries to adopt nearly identical organizational charts, regardless of what each company actually produces. He argues that a company's structure should be designed specifically to support its output, not to mirror conventional corporate norms. However, this logic faces renewed scrutiny given recent events. Huang's unplanned departure — even though brief — demonstrated real vulnerability in a company without a clear transition plan, raising concerns among investors and governance experts who argue that relying on one irreplaceable leader introduces significant risk. Critics suggest that no matter how unconventional or efficient a company's structure may be, a succession plan is a basic safeguard that protects shareholders, employees, and the company's long-term stability. This tension between Huang's vision of a lean, hierarchy-free organization and the practical risks of depending entirely on a single leader is likely to remain a point of debate among Nvidia's board and investors, especially as the company continues to grow in influence across the global technology and AI industries.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Nvidia, a company whose chips power much of the world's artificial intelligence infrastructure, recently experienced a brief but consequential leadership disruption. CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to extramarital affairs, one of which reportedly involved an individual suspected by U.S. authorities of having ties to Chinese intelligence gathering. During Huang's short absence, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress served as interim CEO for 12 days before he resumed his role. Upon returning, Huang held a company-wide meeting addressing the controversy directly — reportedly discussing personal regret, his decision to seek therapy, and the company's code of conduct, the internal guidelines meant to regulate professional behavior among employees and leadership. He also revisited a particularly contentious issue: succession planning, the practice of formally designating who would assume leadership if a CEO departs unexpectedly, whether due to resignation, health issues, or misconduct. According to a source present at the meeting who spoke to CNBC, Huang reiterated his long-held belief that Nvidia does not need such a plan, arguing that formalizing one would introduce unnecessary layers of hierarchy that conflict with the company's operating philosophy. This stance is notable given the circumstances: Huang's own unplanned, if temporary, departure arguably demonstrated exactly the kind of leadership vulnerability that succession planning is designed to mitigate. Nvidia's organizational structure is genuinely unconventional among large corporations. Rather than maintaining the multiple executive tiers and extensive middle management typical of companies its size, Nvidia functions with just five executive officers total, including Huang. He personally oversees around 60 direct reports, a structure that eliminates many traditional layers of corporate bureaucracy. Huang has defended this design philosophy in prior public interviews, arguing that companies should build organizational structures tailored to what they actually produce, rather than defaulting to conventional corporate hierarchies that look similar across unrelated industries, from food service to software to automobiles. From his perspective, the flat structure is not a weakness but a deliberate strategy intended to keep the company fast, adaptive, and efficient. However, this reasoning has not satisfied all stakeholders. Investors, corporate governance analysts, and market watchers argue that succession planning exists precisely to protect companies, employees, and shareholders from the risks inherent in depending heavily on a single irreplaceable leader — risks that became very real when Huang's position was abruptly destabilized by personal scandal. Critics contend that even an unconventional, highly successful company benefits from contingency planning, particularly one as influential and valuable as Nvidia, which plays a central role in the global AI and semiconductor industries. The unresolved tension between Huang's philosophy of minimal hierarchy and the practical demand for institutional safeguards illustrates a broader question facing modern corporations: how much organizational resilience should be sacrificed in the name of efficiency, and what obligations do powerful leaders have to prepare their companies for a future that does not include them.

questions: Do you think a company should always have a backup plan for leadership, even if its leader believes it isn't necessary? Why or why not?

How might trust be affected when a powerful leader makes serious personal mistakes but keeps their job? Can you think of examples from school, sports, or other organizations where trust was tested in a similar way?

If you were in charge of a large company or organization, would you want a simple, flat leadership structure like Nvidia's, or a more traditional one with many layers of managers? What are the risks and benefits of each?
